dedupe_keys.name: carbon dioxide pipelines and marginalised communities in the united states

description: This study by Julia Davis, Nafiseh Salehi, Liqing Li and Majid Shafiee-Jood of the University of Virginia and Texas A&M University, published in Communications Earth & Environment in 2025, examines the environmental justice implications of existing and potential carbon dioxide pipelines in the United States, which carbon capture and removal would require to expand. Coverage: census tract demographic data combined with pipeline spatial data for existing pipelines, proposed pipelines and the Net Zero America study's 2030 projection; LASSO regression selects demographic variables that enter binary logistic regression models. Higher-income communities are less likely to host existing pipelines; proposed pipelines are generally in areas with more Black residents and less likely where educational attainment is higher; in the 2030 projection the effects of income and education weaken and Black residents are less likely to have a pipeline; all pipelines are more likely in rural areas. Format and access: an open article. Licence and cost: free under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Caveats: associations, not exposure or risk; the abstract was the part read. The tract-level predictors can weight equity in pipeline routing and hazard exposure scenarios. It relates to the proposed gas pipelines study and the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index in the catalogue.
